1.title: "Hidden Sweetness": A Long-Standing Consumer Confusion
1.html:
Alsace wine has a long-criticised feature: even when the label gives no information on sweetness, many Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer wines (especially from late-picked grapes or warm vintages) in fact carry clearly perceptible residual sugar yet still go to market as "ordinary AOC Alsace" — a gap with the consumer's intuitive expectation that "white wine = dry", and the root of the long-standing confusion of "is it sweet or not?" that Alsace wine has carried in international markets.

This problem is no accident: Alsace regulations (unlike Germany's) do not require a sugar level at harvest to correspond to a specific sweetness ceiling, and apart from the clear thresholds for VT / SGN, the sweetness of ordinary AOC Alsace depends entirely on the estate's winemaking philosophy and market positioning.
2.title: The 2020 Sweetness Scale: Four-Level Labels Take Effect
2.html:
In response to this long-running controversy, the Alsace wine trade body pushed through a major reform in 2020: from the 2021 vintage, labels of AOC Alsace and AOC Alsace Grand Cru must carry the official sweetness scale (Indication de la Teneur en Sucre):

LevelEnglishStyle
SecDryLowest residual sugar (about 4 g/L or less, relaxed to 9 g/L when acidity is sufficient), a crisp palate
Demi-secOff-dryA slightly soft, gentle sweetness (about 12 g/L or less)
MoelleuxMedium-sweetA clearly sweet, mellow palate (about 12–45 g/L)
DouxSweetRich honeyed sweetness (about 45 g/L or more)

This reform finally lets consumers grasp a wine's sweetness positioning at the point of purchase, without relying on variety stereotypes or the estate's reputation to guess.
3.title: Two Winemaking Philosophies: The Traditional Full School vs the Modern Dry School
3.items.0.label: The Traditional Full Residual-Sugar School
3.items.0.desc: Holds that the natural character of rich varieties such as Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer is suited to keeping some residual sugar to balance their rich body and lowish acidity — stressing "the natural expression of terroir fully ripened", and not deliberately pursuing fermentation to dryness
3.items.1.label: The Modern Ultra-Dry School
3.items.1.desc: Advocates full fermentation to dryness, letting variety and site character come through a pure acid backbone, closer to the international market's expectation of "food-friendly white wine" — a trend that has been rising gradually since the late 1990s, represented especially by younger-generation estates and export-oriented producers
4.title: Both Schools Coexist: Diversity Is the Charm of Alsace
4.html:
Today these two philosophies run side by side in Alsace: some long-established estates still insist on keeping the variety's natural fullness and slightly sweet finish, seeing it as part of the "honest expression of terroir"; while many new-generation estates and export-oriented estates seeking international recognition tend to ferment the wine through to dryness, pursuing a crisp, modern style.

The greatest significance of the 2020 sweetness scale lies not in "eliminating" either style, but in letting both philosophies state their positioning honestly and transparently — when tasting Alsace white wines, forming the habit of looking at the sweetness label first and then judging the tasting context is a key step in understanding the complexity of this region.
5.question: What problem did the new sweetness scale pushed through by the Alsace wine trade body in 2020 mainly solve?
5.options.0: The problem of unclear vineyard classification
5.options.1: The long-standing confusion caused by labels giving no sweetness information, making it hard for consumers to judge how much residual sugar a "dry" wine really has
5.options.2: It abolished the sweetness thresholds for VT and SGN
5.options.3: It required all Alsace white wines to be dry
5.explanation: Alsace has long had a controversy over "hidden sweetness": many Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer wines may carry clear residual sugar even when no sweetness is stated, making it hard for consumers to judge. From the 2021 vintage the 2020 rule makes it mandatory for AOC Alsace and AOC Alsace Grand Cru to state one of four sweetness levels, sec / demi-sec / moelleux / doux, letting both winemaking philosophies state their positioning honestly and transparently.
